name: WingPilot – Your AI Site Consultant & Security Expert
author: ilyag

sections.description:
WingPilot is the WordPress plugin half of WPPilot, an AI site manager that actually knows your site.

On the two names: WingPilot is this plugin — the name in the WordPress.org directory, the folder it installs to, and its text domain. WPPilot is the service it connects to, and the name you’ll see in your wp-admin menu and at getwppilot.com. Everything below that says “WPPilot” is describing the service.

WPPilot reads every page, post, and plugin on your site, builds a structured model of what your site is and who it’s for, then writes you a Briefing — a magazine-quality assessment of what’s working, what isn’t, and where to start.

What WPPilot does once connected:

  • The Briefing — A deep, editorial-quality analysis of your site delivered in the first 90 seconds. Not a checklist. Not a score. A real assessment written in clear language, with specific recommendations you can act on immediately.
  • Conversational actions — Ask WPPilot to rewrite a post title, improve an excerpt, update a meta description, fix typos in body content, or unpublish stale content. Every change shows you a preview first (current vs. proposed, with rationale), and every change can be rolled back with one click. Nothing happens without your approval.
  • Multi-site cockpit — Manage your WordPress sites from a single WPPilot account. The cockpit at app.getwppilot.com shows each site’s status, recent findings, and Briefing insights at a glance. The Free and Starter plans include WPPilot’s AI on one site; Pro and Agency include more.
  • Watchtower monitoring — WPPilot watches your site for security issues, content drift, and structural problems. Findings surface in the cockpit with severity indicators and timestamps. On the Free plan, Watchtower scans weekly; paid plans scan more often.
  • Activity feed — Every action WPPilot takes is logged with timestamps in the cockpit. Roll back any change. Full transparency, full reversibility.
  • Safe by design — The plugin changes your site only when you approve a change in WPPilot. It sends site data (content, metadata, plugin list) to the WPPilot service for analysis, and every change goes through preview → approve → execute, with a one-click undo. You approve every change individually.

What the plugin does locally:

The plugin registers your site’s REST API endpoints so the WPPilot service can read content and, when you approve an action, write changes. It maintains the secure connection (per-site cryptographic secret + JWT authentication) and provides the settings page where you manage the connection.

What is free. The Free plan connects one site, writes your Briefing, shows what needs attention, answers your questions about your site, and completes a limited number of real, approved improvements each month — no credit card required. Paid plans (Starter, Pro, Agency) add more usage and daily monitoring; Pro adds improvements WPPilot finds and prepares for you, and WooCommerce store insights. The plugin itself has no locked features: the limits are those of the WPPilot service, listed at getwppilot.com/pricing.

External Services

This plugin requires a connection to the WPPilot service to function. The plugin’s core value (the Briefing, conversational actions, AI analysis, Watchtower monitoring) is provided by that external service. Without a connection, the plugin provides no standalone functionality other than displaying and receiving the lead forms already placed on your pages; messages sent through those forms stay on your site and are never sent to the WPPilot service.

Below is every service this plugin, or a request it makes, communicates with, what is sent, and when.

1. WPPilot service — api.getwppilot.com

Operated by WPPilot. Your site sends requests to it, and it reads from and (with your approval) writes to your site through the plugin’s REST API (/wp-json/wppilot/v1/), authenticated by a per-site secret and a short-lived token.

What is sent:

  • Site URL, WordPress and PHP versions, timezone, active plugins and themes with their versions and available updates.
  • Post and page content (titles, excerpts, body text, page-builder data, metadata, publish date and author display name), menus, theme styles, Site Health facts and scheduled-task names — when the service requests them, for example to build the Briefing or preview a change.
  • Where a piece of text you ask about appears on your site, when you use WPPilot’s site-wide find: the posts, menus and widgets it appears in with a short surrounding snippet, and the names (never the values) of settings, theme settings and custom fields that contain it, with counts.
  • A list of your posts, pages or products of one type, when you ask about all of them: each item’s title, status, dates, lengths of its text and SEO description (not the text itself), whether it has a featured image, its language and translation group, and for WooCommerce products the SKU, stock status and price. Order, coupon, subscription, form-entry and lead records are never listed.
  • Comments waiting for moderation, when you use comment moderation: each commenter’s name and website URL, the domain of their email address (never the full address), the comment text, and the post it was left on. Commenters’ IP addresses and browser details are not sent.
  • The HTML of one of your public pages, when the service asks for it because a CDN or firewall in front of your site turned its own request away — the plugin requests that page from your site as an anonymous visitor (no login, no cookies), so it is only what any visitor already receives.
  • Site activity events as they happen, so the service can show you an activity feed: logins (username and role), failed login attempts (the username or email address that was typed), user and role changes (username), new comments (the commenter’s name) and comment moderation, plugin and theme changes, post edits, uploads, and changes to a few security-relevant settings such as the site address or the default user role (the setting’s name only).
  • Security scanning data: a list of scannable files with their sizes, timestamps and fingerprints, and the contents of files that are new or have changed since the previous scan, so malware detection can run on the service (see “What is NOT sent” below).
  • Your WordPress admin email address, in the body of the request your site makes each time you click Connect, Finish connecting or Open WPPilot. WPPilot uses it only to propose your account address while no WPPilot account owns the site; you can change it before confirming. It is never put in a web address.

When data is sent:

  • When you click Connect, Reconnect, Finish connecting or Open WPPilot in wp-admin.
  • While the WPPilot admin page is open (connection status, recent activity, Briefing summary).
  • Continuously, as activity events occur on your site while it is connected.
  • During periodic heartbeats and scheduled security scans (approximately daily).
  • When the WPPilot service requests content through the plugin’s REST API.
  • When you approve a change in WPPilot (the service sends the change to the plugin’s REST API).
  • When you delete the plugin: a one-time notice that the connection has ended.

Terms of Use: https://getwppilot.com/terms — Privacy Policy: https://getwppilot.com/privacy

2. WPPilot web app — app.getwppilot.com

When you click Connect, Finish connecting or Open WPPilot, your browser opens the WPPilot app. The address carries your site’s URL, a single-use sign-in token that expires after a few minutes, and the WPPilot page to open. Your site’s server sends nothing to the app itself. Same Terms of Use and Privacy Policy as above.

3. Image sources — Pexels and Openverse

When you approve a new page or post that WPPilot illustrated with a stock photograph, your site downloads that image from where it is hosted and adds it to your own media library, so your page does not depend on someone else’s server. WPPilot chooses images from Pexels (hosted at images.pexels.com) and from Openverse, a WordPress.org project that indexes openly licensed images hosted elsewhere (for example Flickr and Wikimedia Commons); the download goes to the host the image came from, over https only. The plugin accepts only https image addresses and keeps only image files, through WordPress’s own media functions. Nothing about your site is sent other than what any image download reveals: your server’s IP address and WordPress’s standard user agent, which includes your site’s address. Nothing is downloaded until you approve the content.

  • Pexels: Terms — Privacy Policy
  • Openverse: Terms — Privacy Policy; each image’s original host has its own terms, linked from the image’s Openverse page.

4. Your own site

Two features make requests to your own site, not to a third party: after a change, the plugin requests the changed page once to see whether a cache in front of your site still serves the old copy; and the public-page read described above fetches one of your published pages as an anonymous visitor.

What is NOT sent

File contents are transmitted only from the directories that hold distributed software — WordPress core, plugins, themes and must-use plugins — and only for code files. This is a property of where a file lives, not a guess about what is inside it, which is what makes it dependable.

Everything else is inspected on your server, and only the finding is reported. That includes:

  • wp-config.php and any other configuration file — still checked for injected or malicious code, because that is exactly where such code hides; its contents are never sent, so your database credentials and WordPress security keys never leave your server.
  • .htaccess, .user.ini and similar server configuration.
  • Everything in your uploads directory.
  • Every data file — .json, .xml, .txt — wherever it lives, since these are where exported settings, service-account keys and pasted credentials collect.
  • Private keys, certificates and key stores; database dumps, SQL files and archives; .env, .htpasswd and similar credential stores. These are never read for content at all.

For those files, what travels is a statement rather than the file: for example “this file contains two eval() calls, the first on line 14″. No file content, no values, no credentials.

Also never sent: WordPress user passwords or password hashes, commenters’ full email and IP addresses, messages received through WPPilot forms or through Elementor forms (WPPilot reads only how many each Elementor form has kept, never what visitors wrote), and the contents of your database’s options table.

Files whose contents stay on your server are still fingerprinted, so if one is added or altered you are still told.

An honest limitation. Within plugin and theme source code, which is transmitted, a developer who stored a credential directly in their own PHP file may have that line sent. WPPilot removes the ones it can recognise, but it cannot promise to recognise every name a developer might choose. Configuration files — where credentials actually belong, and where yours are — are covered by the boundary above rather than by that recognition.

A free account is required at app.getwppilot.com to use this plugin. Accounts are created during the connect flow, proposing your WordPress admin email address, which you can change before confirming.
sections.installation:
1. Install directly from the WordPress plugin directory, or upload the wingpilot folder to /wp-content/plugins/.
  2. Activate the plugin through the Plugins menu in WordPress.
  3. Open WPPilot from the main wp-admin menu and click Connect to WPPilot. WPPilot opens in a new tab.
  4. Click Authorize in the new tab. An account is created automatically with your WordPress admin email — confirm or change it. That completes the connection.

(Prefer to connect manually? The WPPilot admin page also shows your Site Secret with a Copy button under “Connection details”, so you can paste your site URL + secret at app.getwppilot.com instead.)

Your Briefing will be ready in about 90 seconds.
sections.faq:
Do I need an account?

Yes. A free account at app.getwppilot.com is required. The account is created automatically the first time you connect a site — you’ll confirm your email address as part of the connect flow. The plugin connects your WordPress site to the WPPilot service; without the connection, the only thing it does on its own is keep any WPPilot forms on your pages working.

What data does the plugin send?

Site metadata (URL, WordPress/PHP versions, plugin list, theme), content (titles, excerpts, body text) when requested by the service, comments awaiting moderation when you use that feature, activity events while your site is connected, and security scanning data. Your WordPress admin email is sent to WPPilot in the body of the request each time you click Connect or Open WPPilot, so it can be proposed as your account address while no account owns the site; it is never put in a web address. See the full External Services disclosure above.

Security scanning still reads the files attackers actually modify — wp-config.php included, since skipping it would make for a poor security product. What it does not do is send them. Files outside WordPress core, plugin and theme code are inspected on your own server, and only the finding travels: “this file contains executable code it should not”, never the file. Private keys, database dumps, archives and credential stores are not read for content at all. See the full External Services disclosure above.

Can WPPilot change things on my site?

Only with your explicit approval, and only your content. The changes the plugin can make are: post and page titles, excerpts, body content and status; SEO titles and meta descriptions; new draft pages and posts (including Elementor pages); text in Elementor, Beaver Builder and Bricks layouts; image alt text and approved stock images added to your media library; menu item labels and links; comment moderation and a post’s discussion settings; custom field values; WPPilot lead forms; and clearing Elementor’s generated CSS after a change. Each change is checked against the permissions of the WordPress user who connected the site, never adds scripts or PHP, shows you a preview first, and can be rolled back from the activity feed in the cockpit.

Does WingPilot install plugins or run code?

No. It never downloads, installs, activates or updates plugins, themes or code, and never runs code it receives. If you want more than this plugin does, you can optionally install the separate WPPilot Advanced add-on yourself from the WPPilot app; nothing is installed or pushed to your site automatically.

Can I manage multiple sites from one account?

Yes. Install and connect WingPilot on each WordPress site you want WPPilot to manage. All sites connected with the same account email appear in your cockpit at app.getwppilot.com.

Can I disconnect at any time?

Yes. Open WPPilot from the main wp-admin menu and click Emergency Disconnect (you’ll be asked to confirm). This immediately revokes all tokens and stops all backend communication. The plugin becomes inert. You can also disconnect individual sites from the cockpit at app.getwppilot.com.

How do I try WPPilot on a test site?

Install and activate the plugin on a site that is reachable from the internet, open WPPilot in wp-admin and click Connect to WPPilot, then Authorize in the tab that opens. Your Briefing follows in about 90 seconds; ask WPPilot to rewrite a post title to see a change previewed, approved and then undone from the activity feed.

Does the plugin work on localhost?

For the full experience, your site needs to be accessible from the internet so the WPPilot backend can reach the plugin’s REST API. For local development, you can use a tunnel service like ngrok to expose your local site.

Where do form messages go, and what happens to them if I delete the plugin?

Each message sent through a WPPilot form is emailed to the address set for that form and saved under WPPilot → Leads in wp-admin. Saved leads stay on your site — they are not sent to the WPPilot service. Forms work whether or not your site is connected. If you delete the plugin, the form settings are removed but your saved leads are kept.

What WordPress versions are supported?

WordPress 6.0 and above, tested through 7.1, with PHP 8.0 or higher.

Is WPPilot free?

Yes, there’s a free tier — install, connect, get your Briefing, and try the conversational actions without a credit card. Paid tiers (Starter, Pro, Agency) unlock higher usage limits and additional capabilities; see getwppilot.com for current pricing.
sections.changelog:
1.6.0

  • First release in the WordPress.org directory. Copies installed from getwppilot.com keep their connection and settings, and take their updates from WordPress.org from this version on.
  • Fixed: after WPPilot was updated, the next step of the update (or a background request in the admin) could be redirected to WPPilot’s page instead of finishing. Only a first install now opens WPPilot’s page, and only on an ordinary admin page.
  • The plans summary on the WPPilot page now lists what paid plans actually add.
  • Security: a new Elementor page, and any change to page text or a page-builder layout, can no longer add a script or event handler, including in place of one that was already there. WPPilot no longer changes the body or status of anything that is not site content, such as Additional CSS or another plugin’s code, and publishing a new page needs the permission to publish.

1.5.31

  • Fixed: on hosts that switch off some PHP functions (such as disk_free_space), WPPilot could not read your site’s environment or its plugin and theme list, and answered without them. It now reads both on those hosts too.

1.5.30

  • Security: a change WPPilot makes to the words on a Beaver Builder or Bricks page is now refused if it would add a script, an event handler (such as onclick) or a script address, exactly as changes to a page body and to Elementor layouts already were. The same check now also covers custom fields and settings that hold page text. Markup the text already held is kept; nothing unsafe is added, by a change or by its undo.
  • Fixed: undoing a move to the trash no longer gives a post an address another post took in the meantime. Before, the post came back sharing that address (as a draft) or renamed with “-2” (when published). Now WPPilot says the address is taken and leaves the post in the trash, with nothing changed.
  • New: when you ask where your form enquiries go, WPPilot now reads the notification recipients saved by Contact Form 7, WPForms, Formidable Forms and Gravity Forms (read-only), and names the site admin address where a form sends to it by default.

1.5.29

  • Fixed: a change WPPilot makes to a page or post body now stores exactly what you approved. Before, block settings WordPress keeps escaped (an &, a quote, < or -- inside a block’s settings) lost their backslashes when saved, and a title, excerpt, new draft or meta description lost any backslash it contained.
  • Fixed: WPPilot no longer changes a WooCommerce order as if it were a post. On stores that keep orders in their own tables, an order’s number also names a placeholder post that is not the order; changing that post’s status changed nothing about the order while reporting that it had. Orders, and any item whose type no active plugin registers, are now refused with the reason, and nothing is changed.

1.5.28

  • Improved: when WPPilot changes a menu item’s label or link, it now records the item’s date along with its place in the menu, so undoing the change can confirm the item is back exactly where and as it was.

1.5.27

  • Improved: when WPPilot answers a question about a whole set of your content — how many products are out of stock, which listings are duplicates, which pages have no meta description or no translation — your site now counts every item itself, so the numbers cover all of them even on a large or slow site where reading every item in time is not possible.

1.5.26

  • Fixed: changing a menu item’s label or link now changes only that label or link. Before, saving the item also reset its date and could move an item to the end of its menu, and undoing the change put the label back but not its place.

1.5.25

  • Fixed: changing a menu item’s label or link no longer moves it. Before, the renamed item left its submenu for the top level of the menu and could change places with its neighbours, and WPPilot then refused to undo the change because the item was no longer where it had been.
  • Before WPPilot moves a post to the trash, it can now tell you how many of its comments are approved, waiting, spam or in the trash, since they are hidden along with the post.

1.5.24

  • Security: the checks that keep scripts out of page content now read markup the way a browser does. An encoded address such as javascript:, a tab inside one, or an event handler separated by a slash (<img/src=x/onerror=…>) is refused like its plain spelling, for page and post bodies and for Elementor layouts. An Elementor layout can no longer gain a script, an event handler or a scripting address it did not already have.
  • WPPilot’s changes to an Elementor layout, and their undo, are now written only while the layout still holds what WPPilot read, so they never overwrite an edit made in the meantime.

1.5.23

  • WPPilot can now go through every item of one kind at once — every tour, product, page or post — instead of a sample, so “how many products are out of stock?” or “which tours have no meta description?” gets an answer about all of them. It reads titles, statuses, whether an excerpt, meta description (in your SEO plugin’s own field) and featured image are set, WooCommerce stock, price and SKU, and Polylang or WPML language versions. Never page text. Read-only: nothing is changed. Only an administrator’s connection can run it.

1.5.22

  • Fixed: undoing a change that moved a post or page to the trash now brings back its comments too, each in the status it had (waiting, approved or spam). Before, the post came back and its comments stayed hidden with the trashed post.
  • WPPilot no longer moves a post to the trash on a site whose trash is switched off, where WordPress would delete it permanently instead.

1.5.21

  • WPPilot can now tell you where a piece of text is stored across your whole site — an old domain, a phone number, a name — with how many times it appears in each place: page and post content (drafts and scheduled posts included), Elementor layouts (where button and link addresses are stored with their slashes escaped), custom fields, menus, widgets, Customizer settings and other settings. It also says what it did not search. Read-only: nothing is changed. Only an administrator’s connection can run it; passwords, keys and anything stored under a credential-like name are counted but never quoted.

1.5.20

  • WPPilot can now change a custom field on a post or page — for example one day of a tour’s itinerary kept in an ACF, Pods, Meta Box or JetEngine field — after you approve it, with undo. Only the one value you asked about changes: the other rows and sub-fields of the field are written back exactly as they were, the field is checked again just before it changes (anything you changed yourself in the meantime is left alone), ACF fields are saved through ACF itself, and undo puts back exactly what was there. Fields WordPress or a plugin keeps for itself, passwords and keys, fields that link to other content or media, and anything stored as a PHP object are never changed this way.

1.5.19

  • When WPPilot reads a post or page, it now also reads the post’s custom fields — the itinerary, price lists, specifications and other details that sites built with Pods, ACF, Meta Box, JetEngine or Toolset keep outside the main content and show through their templates. Before, a page whose words all live in custom fields looked empty to WPPilot even though visitors saw it in full. Fields are read with their labels where the field plugin provides them; passwords and anything shaped like a key or credential are never sent, and only users who can edit the post have its fields read.
  • When your homepage’s search title comes from your site title and tagline, WPPilot now reads what changing them would reach on your site — each language version of the homepage, with the tagline as that language shows it under Polylang or WPML, and the title of another page — instead of assuming it, so it can prepare the homepage title you asked for and tell you exactly what else it changes.

Earlier versions are listed in changelog.txt, included with the plugin.

File contents are transmitted only from the directories that hold distributed software — WordPress core, plugins, themes and must-use plugins — and only for code files. This is a property of where a file lives, not a guess about what is inside it, which is what makes it dependable.

Everything else is inspected on your server, and only the finding is reported. That includes:

  • wp-config.php and any other configuration file — still checked for injected or malicious code, because that is exactly where such code hides; its contents are never sent, so your database credentials and WordPress security keys never leave your server.
  • .htaccess, .user.ini and similar server configuration.
  • Everything in your uploads directory.
  • Every data file — .json, .xml, .txt — wherever it lives, since these are where exported settings, service-account keys and pasted credentials collect.
  • Private keys, certificates and key stores; database dumps, SQL files and archives; .env, .htpasswd and similar credential stores. These are never read for content at all.

For those files, what travels is a statement rather than the file: for example “this file contains two eval() calls, the first on line 14″. No file content, no values, no credentials.

Also never sent: WordPress user passwords or password hashes, commenters’ full email and IP addresses, messages received through WPPilot forms or through Elementor forms (WPPilot reads only how many each Elementor form has kept, never what visitors wrote), and the contents of your database’s options table.

Files whose contents stay on your server are still fingerprinted, so if one is added or altered you are still told.

An honest limitation. Within plugin and theme source code, which is transmitted, a developer who stored a credential directly in their own PHP file may have that line sent. WPPilot removes the ones it can recognise, but it cannot promise to recognise every name a developer might choose. Configuration files — where credentials actually belong, and where yours are — are covered by the boundary above rather than by that recognition.

A free account is required at app.getwppilot.com to use this plugin. Accounts are created during the connect flow, proposing your WordPress admin email address, which you can change before confirming.
